0: 'I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan; in the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.'
2: It is an oath by the war-horses that served in the defense of Islam — an oath by these steeds in their various states: as they gallop panting, as their hooves strike sparks from the rock, and as those swift chargers raid the attacking enemy and charge into their midst at dawn, raising dust on the battlefield. This oath refers back to the jihad of the warriors. As for camels and beasts of burden, they were mentioned in Surah al-Nahl: 'and horses, mules and donkeys, that you may ride them' (Quran 16:8) — recalled there as divine blessings, not as objects of an oath. Likewise of the flocks He said: 'and for you there is beauty in them when you bring them in and when you send them out' (Quran 16:6) — this is the beauty of herding.
8: 'Islam is exalted and nothing is exalted above it' — a declarative sentence delivered with the intent of a command.
9: This — 'that He may make it prevail over all religion' (Quran 9:33; also 48:28, 61:9) — though outwardly a report, is delivered with performative intent. And in the close of Surah al-Bayyina, that the believers and God-fearing are the best of people on earth — the best, most upright, most learned civilization — He said 'they are the best of creation' (Quran 98:7). The truly righteous (abrar) are not merely those who do good deeds; the man of birr is he whose heart is open like the vast plains, unbounded — who says, 'O God, forgive me and all believing men and women in the easts and wests of the earth,' and, 'It is not sweet for me to rest while in the farthest reach of my rule there is an orphan, a hungry one, or one in distress.' He is the man of birr.
10: 'Bariyya' means 'the created,' so you Muslims are the best of creatures — on condition that a person struggles against disbelief, colonialism and tyranny, whether by the pen or by action. These declarative sentences are delivered with performative intent: 'you are the best of creation.' It addresses a universal principle to the listener, without preface or command.
11: Without 'By the chargers panting, striking sparks, raiding at dawn, raising therein a cloud of dust' (Quran 100:1-4) — without struggle, without jihad — or with them.
12: If it is with these, then it becomes 'the best of creation' — the best civilization is yours, the best culture is yours, the best life is yours.
14: In the close of Surah al-Bayyina came 'those who believe and do righteous deeds — they are the best of creation' (Quran 98:7). Such statements, though a promise, carry a definite command: you must have the best civilization, nation, law, and leader — the imam of the community whom He has appointed — and its measure is the Qur'an and the Pure Ones (the Ahl al-Bayt).
18: The praise, exaltation and honor God gives the human being go back to his primordial nature (fitra) — to that universal covenant: 'And when your Lord took from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes' (Quran 7:172). All virtue and excellence go back to that dimension.
19: And all flaws and defects go back to 'man was created' — this human being made from clay/mire (lajin) goes back to that.
20: He said 'he indeed fails who buries it' (Quran 91:10): if someone buries the divine fitra that testified 'Yes' at the great covenant, stops its mouth and will not let it speak, then his spokesman becomes his caprice and desire; he moves by conjecture and inclination. Even if he outwardly denies the Origin, in his own conscience he affirms it and within himself he is a witness — for the fitra cannot be destroyed; it is alive, only intrigued against and silenced.
21: It is knowing and aware; it sees, knows, and can speak; and on the Day of Resurrection the human being testifies against himself: 'witnessing against themselves that they disbelieved' (Quran 9:17).
22: As the limbs bear witness, so does the fitra against this human — who smothered the fitra and let his animal nature flourish; who is 'ungrateful to his Lord' (Quran 100:6), 'and to that he is a witness' (Quran 100:7), and 'and violent in his love of wealth' (Quran 100:8). 'Wealth' is not only property: it is rank, position, leadership. Man uses all that is on the earth — mineral, plant, animal, human — as tools. As in Surah Al 'Imran: 'beautified for people is the love of desires — of women and sons, and heaped hoards of gold and silver' (Quran 3:14).
23: 'and branded horses, and cattle and tillage' (Quran 3:14): 'harth' (tillage) is agriculture; 'branded horses and cattle' are livestock; the 'heaped hoards' are gold, silver, precious objects and antiquities — the mineral; and 'sons and women' are the human.
24: The heaped hoards pertain to the mineral, the branded horses and cattle to animal husbandry, tillage to plants, and 'women and sons' to the human. He presses all four — human, plant, mineral, animal — into service as tools. When this person enters the Resurrection, his first witness is his fitra: 'witnessing against themselves that they disbelieved' (Quran 9:17).
25: Bear in mind that the witness is other than the accused. This self, when its fitra — 'he fails who buries it' (Quran 91:10)...
26: ...concealed it and buried it amid appetites and instincts until it died — yet it is within him, his very self; this same fitra was present at 'Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes' (Quran 7:172). Now that it has come to this state, this human who...
28: He has imprisoned his fitra within its own house; then he himself becomes the wrongdoer. More than fifty times in the Noble Qur'an God describes him: ungrateful, a witness against himself, violent in love of wealth, a schemer; he develops problems of belief and of injustice. 'when kings enter a town they ruin it and make its mighty people humbled' (Quran 27:34) is of this kind. These fifty-odd censures pertain to the empty half of the human, for he has buried the full half. On the Day of Resurrection the first thing to testify against the deceived human is 'witnessing against themselves that they disbelieved' — this is the very sentence about the fitra.
29: Some of the great scholars interpreted it thus: the human who has taken an animal's form — his whole being testifies against himself that he is a plunderer; this is a practical testimony. The first witness is the household witness ('witnessing against themselves'); then it reaches the limbs: 'their tongues testify against them for what they did' (Quran 24:24). Testimony is other than confession: if the criminal speaks, that is confession; if an outsider speaks against him, that is testimony. We are other than our hand, foot, skin and flesh. The hand that gives or takes bribes over and under the table is a tool of action.
30: So the hand testifies that this person took and gave. The Qur'an does not say the hand confessed; it says the hand testified — so the self of the human is the one who gives and takes; the sin belongs to the human, to his empty half, which goes back to 'sounding clay of molded mire' (Quran 15:26), while the other half goes back to the divine in-breathing (nafkh). Testimony may be external, or internal — the fitra against nature, or the limbs against nature. The nature-bound human who is 'violent in love of wealth' must return to 'Say: if you love God, follow me, and God will love you' (Quran 3:31) — the pre-eternal Beloved, who is God; and God said to His beloved: Say...
32: It is mineral, plant, animal and human, and he attaches his heart to them. After smothering his fitra — 'he fails who buries it' (Quran 91:10) — he behaves without courtesy toward God Most Holy, becomes ill-mannered and immoral; and his own faculties testify against him. This fitra does not die; it endures, though imprisoned — 'and to that he is a witness' (Quran 100:7).
35: The human himself knows that when we exhume the grave and what is in the breast comes onto the table, he — who was aware — says: 'What is this record that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it?' (Quran 18:49). They can hide nothing.
36: He is aware now; the inner witness is present, though he buried it — 'he buried it.' 'What is this record that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it?' (Quran 18:49) — the great ledgers are with God and the divine administrators; but the ordinary register that seems 'forgotten' is not lost: 'a soul will know what it has brought present' (Quran 81:14) — the human carries it with himself.
37: As for what another records — the noble scribes 'noble writers' (Quran 82:11) also record it — but 'a soul will know what it brought' (Quran 81:14): an indefinite noun here yields general meaning, so 'every soul will know what it has brought present'; the human himself will make it present. So although these verses have been linked to Hajj and the pilgrim-camels, the primary reading pertains to the matters of jihad; and it makes the human aware that he has a master of the house who witnesses his deeds and has recorded them.
